summary:
Lunar Echoes is an educational digital museum that tells the stories of NASA hardware left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Built for the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge, it introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the machines, instruments and technology that completed their missions and that explored other worlds and were left behind on them or in space.

Visitors can browse a filterable gallery of missions, explore a chronological timeline, open detailed pages with stories, technologies, discoveries and what was left behind, and test their knowledge with a short quiz. All content is grounded in official NASA, JPL, ESA and ISRO open data and images.

The project is a fully static website (HTML, Tailwind CSS, vanilla JavaScript and a single JSON data file), with no backend. It is designed to be fast, accessible and easy to maintain, so the stories of this “ghost” hardware stay visible and understandable for the next generation of explorers.
details:
What it does

Lunar Echoes is a static educational website that presents hardware from NASA and partner missions. Users can:

• filter missions by body (Moon, Mars, Deep Space);

• browse mission cards with summary, year and status;

• follow a chronological timeline;

• open a detail page for each mission (story, why it matters, location, technologies, key discoveries, hardware left behind, and sources);

• take a short quiz to reinforce what they learned.

How it works

All mission data lives in JSON data files. Vanilla JavaScript loads the data (the quiz data is validated question by question), renders the home page (filters, cards, timeline) and the mission detail page (including an image gallery and section navigation). Styling uses Tailwind CSS via CDN plus a small custom stylesheet. There is no server-side code and no database.

Benefits and impact

The site makes the “abandoned” hardware and the science it enabled accessible to school-age audiences and the general public. It shows that these machines still matter: some instruments are still used, others proved techniques that later missions built on, and all of them are part of the history of exploration.

Tools and stack

• HTML5

• Tailwind CSS 3.4.17 (CDN)

• Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+)

• Static JSON (missions_data.json and quiz_data.json)

• ImageMagick for local image preparation

• GitHub Pages for hosting

Creativity

We focused on clear storytelling rather than heavy frameworks: a dark, clean interface, mission cards with body badges, a timeline, a detail page with sticky section navigation, and a quiz. Content is written in accessible English and tied to official NASA, JPL, ESA and ISRO sources. Mission images are local (no external hotlinks at runtime).

Factors considered

Audience (school-age and general public), simple static architecture, accessibility (focus styles, aria attributes, reduced motion), performance (local images under size limits), and data integrity (a documented data format and image size limits).
